item.title: How to Accomplish the Impossible in Six Steps
item.description:
Social Life

How to Accomplish the Impossible in Six Steps

From slavery to civil rights, the impossible can become inevitable. How?

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • History is full of impossibilities come alive: the abolition of slavery; the civil rights laws of the ‘60s.
  • These transformations follow the same six-step arc, from first story to eventual tipping point.
  • The next impossible may well be a return from isolation, coming home to each other using these same six steps.
Source: Franck-Boston / iStock

I’m 18, home on winter break from my first semester at McGill University, and excited to finally see Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home. After an exhausting finals week, I really need a film that reawakens my heart and brings back the laughter, and, luckily, this one does both.

One scene has stuck with me through the years, and here’s how I remember it: the beloved crew of the Enterprise travels back to 1980s San Francisco, where chief engineer Scotty sits down at a desktop computer, clears his throat, and says, Computer? When nothing happens, McCoy hands him the mouse and Scotty lifts it to his lips like it’s a microphone: Hello, computer. The audience around me, myself included, bursts into laughter, because of course you can’t talk to a computer; that’s the stuff of science fiction, impossible.

Today, I talk to my computer every day… and it talks back.

Impossibilities Come Alive

History is filled with impossibilities that come to life. In 1903, the New York Times looked at humanity’s failed attempts to build a flying machine and declared it might take from one million to 10 million years, only to see the Wright brothers lift off 69 days later. Then in 1920, the Times wrote that rocket pioneer Robert Goddard seemed to lack the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools (responding to his suggestion that a rocket could fly through space). Forty-nine years later, as Apollo 11 raced toward the moon, the paper printed its retraction: The Times regrets the error.

These impossibilities-turned-real happened, at least in part, because of profit: money invested, confident more money would be returned. But the impossible has also happened without profit, even at its expense, at times when our deepest human needs were going unmet.

If the slave trade is gone… beggars we’ll all become, warned a popular verse in 1790s England. This trade was considered just too profitable to end until, after a 20-year struggle, Britain abolished it in 1807 (and abolished slavery itself 26 years later).

Segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever! declared Alabama governor George Wallace in 1963, defending a system that kept Black workers in the lowest-paying jobs, to the benefit of white business owners (a system its defenders said would be economically disastrous to undo). But by 1965, the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act had become law.

How did these impossibilities happen?

The Impossible in Six Steps

Step 1: Story

It begins with a story. In a well-known study, people gave more to help one named, pictured child (whose face told a story) than they did to help millions described by statistics (Small et al., 2007)… because stories pull us in so completely that their messages slip right past our defenses (Green & Brock, 2000). Consider this: On December 1, 1955, a seamstress took a seat on a Montgomery bus and refused to give it up when the driver ordered her to move for a white passenger. Rosa Parks’s small act of defiance led to her arrest, imprisonment, and conviction.

Step 2: Hidden Majority

Stories like this land on a hidden majority, the many people who privately share the same sentiment but stay silent because they’re certain they’re alone (Prentice & Miller, 1993). In Montgomery, nearly every Black rider had their own tale of bus-system injustice, and now they were hearing it echoed in Rosa Parks’s.

Step 3: Small Circle

A hidden majority doesn’t rise at once, because acting alone is frightening. Instead, change begins in a small, close circle, where people give each other the courage to step forward (Centola, 2010). On the night of Parks’s arrest, one small circle, the Women’s Political Council, led by professor Jo Ann Robinson, decided to act, staying up all night running off leaflets: Don’t ride the bus on Monday. They were hoping 60 percent of Black riders would stay off; nearly all of them did.

Step 4: Social Proof

From here, other circles see the first one doing something brave, and they believe they can be brave too (researchers call this social proof) (Cialdini, 2009; Suh et al., 2017). As reporters spread images of the tens of thousands of people walking miles to get to work in Montgomery, new circles sprang into action in Tallahassee, Birmingham, Atlanta, and Greensboro, and soon one city’s circle had become a web stretching across the South.

Step 5: Persistence

Now comes the long, messy middle, when established systems push back, and the only path forward is patience and persistence. White leaders in the South answered with what they called massive resistance, beating Freedom Riders, leaving protestors and organizers bloody at bus stations, but the circles keep meeting and organizing.

Step 6: Tipping Point

Finally, the promise hidden in sociologist Damon Centola’s research arrives: when those willing to stand up publicly grow and reach about a quarter of the entire group, then the whole group comes to a tipping point and suddenly flips (Centola et al., 2018). In May 1963, Birmingham police turned fire hoses and attack dogs on marching children, and images broadcast into living rooms across the country moved more and more Americans to stand against segregation. Within two years, the impossible had become law.

The Next Impossible: Belonging

The impossible I care deeply about is rebuilding cultures of belonging. For two million years, we lived in villages of 30 to 150 people, sharing work, meals, songs, and sorrows, and our minds became wired for that kind of connection. But today we arrive in a world emptied of this shared life, greeted by two busy parents struggling to do alone what a whole village once shared, and later we’re told to go out and make it on our own… and we all feel the cost in our isolation and exhaustion.

The same process, six steps, can carry us back to a world of belonging. Stories, like that of a six-year-old boy told by his new family to stop grieving the deaths of his mother and brother, and, in sharp contrast, of a young girl held for weeks by her fellow villagers after her father dies, can touch a hidden majority who believe they must carry loneliness and exhaustion all on their own.

These stories can also spark change, beginning in small circles of five to 12 people who feel inspired to rekindle belonging: they start gathering each week for Sunday dinner, three unhurried hours woven with stillness and compassion… and then let their growing care for each other spill out into everyday life, one shared ride, one casserole at a time.

Soon, these circles become visible, and social proof takes hold: one circle emboldens another, and, with persistence, we can reach a tipping point where (much like the original crew of the USS Enterprise in Star Trek IV) we make The Voyage Home… to each other, because belonging and connection are not only our deepest needs; they are our sweetest ending.

item.title: The Hidden Cost of Being the Reliable One
item.description:
Identity

The Hidden Cost of Being the Reliable One

When being the person everyone counts on starts to take a toll

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Being reliable often leads to growing expectations from others and ourselves.
  • Outsourcing tasks doesn't necessarily reduce the mental load of managing them.
  • Stepping back can bring guilt and grief when being needed has become part of one's identity.

Lately, I’ve been hearing some version of the same question from women in midlife: “I’ve done everything I was supposed to do. Is this it?”

Many are navigating perimenopause, changing bodies and identities, and beginning to challenge inherited beliefs. At work, they’re often the “go-to” person who finishes projects. At home, they’re doing the “second shift” of kin-keeping, scheduling appointments, and keeping the family connected. They once believed professional success and increased income would lead to more freedom.

Ironically, the more reliable their reputation, the more they’re expected to handle everything. They often hear, “But you’re just so good at it!”

According to Gallup’s 2026 report, 34 percent of women working full-time were engaged at work, compared with 28 percent of men. Yet 31 percent of women reported frequent workplace burnout, compared with 23 percent of men. This gap was true for women with and without children.

And then there’s perimenopause, about which researchers are only beginning to learn how varied and diverse the symptoms are. A 2025 study following 679 women found that increases in menopause symptoms over six months were associated with increases in burnout.

Add on the return-to-office mandates, job insecurity, and rising costs, and it makes it harder to scale back or imagine doing things differently. A September 2026 CDC report found that 71.5 percent of U.S. adults felt very tired or exhausted at least some days during the previous three months, with women reporting more fatigue than men (20 percent vs 13 percent).

The Promise of Having More Time

Many women, myself included, naively believed that as we advanced in our careers and earned more money, we’d eventually have greater freedom and flexibility. Maybe we could afford to hire help with childcare, cleaning, or food delivery. But even then, women oftentimes are still the ones carrying the mental load of making sure everything gets done.

The women in my practice are smart and capable. They recognize that their own expectations contribute to their exhaustion, but knowing this doesn’t necessarily make it easier to let go. They ask, “Well, if I don’t do it, who will? Who will make lunches or check in on aging parents?” These are valid questions, especially when they’ve been the default caregivers for years.

Many say they no longer want to play the game, yet don’t know how to stop. After all, running and staying ahead have been a big part of their identity.

When Being Dependable Becomes Your Identity

Meet “Julie,” a fictional composite of many high-achieving women I’ve worked with.

Julie is a Gen Xer or elder Millennial who came of age during the “girlboss” and lean-in era. According to LinkedIn, she’s successful. Inside, she’s wondering how long she can keep going.

She has young children and helps care for aging parents. As the oldest daughter, she once took pride in being the glue that kept everyone together. Lately, she’s wondering what it would feel like to have someone else take care of things for a change.

However, when we explore change, four questions usually come up.

What Happens When You Stop Being the Go-to Person?

1. What if everyone gets mad at me?

This is a common one, especially for women who may have been socialized to be “nice” or are used to putting others before themselves. In families or cultures where caring for others is tied to love and responsibility, disappointing others can feel like rejecting and losing relationships.

In our work together, we accept the reality that some people may be upset when dynamics change. They’ve become accustomed to a certain version of you. Our work involves tolerating their disappointment while staying connected to what matters to you.

2. What if something bad happens?

Our brains are so good at imagining all the worst-case scenarios, aren’t they? It’s what helped keep our ancestors alive, but I remind clients it is no longer helping us.

I walk through these scenarios with clients. What’s the worst thing that could happen? How likely is it? And how would you handle it?

Perhaps the kids miss a few servings of vegetables. Maybe the house is messier than you’d like, or someone forgets an appointment. Some things will probably fall through the cracks, but we identify the actual non-negotiables for daily life to function and the “would be nice” and how to tell the difference.

3. Am I a bad person?

For many women, self-worth has long been tied to doing and being in service to others. I help clients move beyond black-and-white thinking about being a good or bad person and consider whether their actions align with their values.

Can you be a caring person who is invested in others’ well-being and decline another volunteer activity?

Can you love your family and decide you no longer want to remind everyone about the reunion?

Often, my clients need someone to hold up a mirror so they can see that they don’t judge others by these same standards.

4. What if I’m no longer needed?

This is an unexpected question for many folks and one they did not realize they were contending with. Letting go of responsibility can bring up unexpected grief.

Oftentimes my clients don’t realize that being the go-to person has brought pride and meaning. Whether an innate ability or a survival tactic, they’ve developed skills in anticipating needs, solving problems, and caring for others.

Stepping back can bring sadness about losing that role or grief over how many years they’ve spent carrying it. We also examine how we may have contributed to these dynamics. Taking accountability can help us recognize where we have the power to make changes.

Making Room for Yourself Again

We’re entering the stretch between Halloween and New Year’s, when days get shorter, and gatherings multiply.

This might be a good time to check in with yourself before answering another request: Is this something I want to do? Is it something others expect me to do? Or is it something I’ve always done?

I remind clients that small, daily actions add up. Maybe it’s letting someone else plan the next gathering, saying no, or asking for help before reaching a breaking point.

If you didn’t have to be the person who holds everything together, what might you have more room for?

item.title: How Well-Roundedness Contributes to Meaningful Lives
item.description:
Philosophy

How Well-Roundedness Contributes to Meaningful Lives

Do well-rounded people avoid the hedonic treadmill?

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Balancing intellectual and sensory pleasures may build happiness, resilience, and social connection.
  • Varied interests may counter the hedonic treadmill by keeping experiences from becoming routine.
  • A hobby can relieve stress, bring joy, and teach acceptance of personal limits, even if you're bad at it.

Review of The Well-Rounded Life. By Amy Berg. Princeton University Press. 237 pp. $27.95.

In his iconic treatise, Utilitarianism, John Stuart Mill claimed that deploying “the higher faculties” was superior to pleasures involving “mere sensation,” which he attributed to an “infirmity of character.”

Source: u d7hddm5o/Pixabay

According to Amy Berg, a professor of philosophy at Rice University, Mill was “wrong, both descriptively and prescriptively.” In The Well-Rounded Life, Berg makes a thought-provoking and compelling case that people who tap both kinds of pleasure and balance them appropriately tend to be more socially connected, resilient, and happier.

Berg acknowledges, however, that well-roundedness is more difficult to achieve for some of us, including the working poor, mothers with small children, and socioeconomically elite men who believe that work is the place to find meaning and fulfillment.

That said, Berg cites a study conducted by a team of psychologists, in which 83 percent of participants described their ideal lives as a balance between work and leisure, with the latter including time spent with family, participation in religious activities, and learning new things.

Being well-rounded, Berg writes, allows us to do justice to our multiple skills, potential talents, and interests, and to “achieve a balance” between and among them. It facilitates the development of relationships, casual and intense, with a diverse set of people, be they bakers, potters or cyclists. Well-roundedness allows us to avoid what psychologists call “the hedonic treadmill,” stimulated by the “same-old, same-old” sets of experiences.

A commitment to well-roundedness also generates opportunities for fruitful cross-pollination. Compared to other scientists, Berg reveals, Nobel Laureates are seven times more likely to be visual artists, sculptors or printmakers; 12 times more likely to write poetry, plays, essays, and books; 22 times more likely to dabble in acting, dance, and magic. Sometimes, Berg speculates, the skills at play in one domain prove to be transferable to another one.

Even being bad at a hobby, she points out, has an upside. It can relieve stress from a demanding job. It can be fun. And in what Berg calls “silver linings perfectionism,” it can develop character when we bump up against the limits of our skills.

To be sure, well-roundedness requires trade-offs. But Berg maintains that ambivalence about choices between competing options “is a sign of a healthy, functioning person.” She encourages anyone who is convinced, for example, that finding a cure for cancer must be his or her life’s work to internalize the value of the space occupied by “playing the oboe, learning to pole vault, or teaching preschool.” And to recognize that, alas, “it is rarely the case” that sacrificing a casual interest will free up the time to write The Great American Novel. For this reason, Berg confesses that she herself “errs on the side of choosing well-being over meaning.”

For most of us, Berg concludes, life “is not as unified”—or as exemplary—as it is in an obituary or a biography. And she encourages her readers not to spend too much of their time “trying to live up to a great story,” i.e., a decision to pursue a goal, the achievement of that goal, and the arc of sacrifices redeemed. All too often, this approach sets conditions that allow far too few of us to clear the bar.

Berg understands that “sometimes we have to put the B plots on the back burner so the A plot can cook.” But she insists as well that most lives “don’t revolve around one or more central projects.” And that accomplishments “that reach the heights of meaning may be out of reach for the ordinary well-rounded person.”

Most importantly, Berg emphasizes that the necessity of making life-changing choices “isn’t only a reason for gloom: it’s a way to learn what really matters to each of us, what kind of life we want to live, what kind of person we want to be.”

item.title: GLP-1 Drugs and Eating Disorders: What Experts Recommend
item.description:
Eating Disorders

GLP-1 Drugs and Eating Disorders: What Experts Recommend

New expert guidance highlights the benefits and risks of GLP-1 medications.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 drugs may benefit some people with binge eating disorder, but evidence remains limited.
  • GLP-1 drugs may trigger restrictive eating or relapse in vulnerable individuals.
  • Screening for eating disorders before prescribing GLP-1 drugs is essential.
  • Weight loss does not equal eating disorder recovery; ongoing monitoring is crucial.

GLP-1 medications, such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, have revolutionized the treatment of Type 2 diabetes and obesity. By reducing appetite, slowing gastric emptying, and promoting significant weight loss, they have generated considerable interest in both the medical field and public opinion.

However, their wider use in the population has raised an important question: What happens when these drugs are prescribed to people with eating disorders or who are at risk of developing them?

A recent consensus article published in World Psychiatry has addressed this question. Using the Delphi method, 45 experts and people with personal experience of eating disorders have elaborated several recommendations for clinical practice and future research.

The principal message of the consensus is that GLP-1 medications can offer several benefits, but they carry potential risks for people with eating disorders. Their use, therefore, requires careful attention, personalized decisions, and continuous monitoring.

Potential Benefits of GLP-1s for Binge Eating Disorder

There is growing interest in the possible use of GLP-1 medications in the treatment of binge-eating disorder (BED). Some studies have found a reduction in binge-eating episodes; however, the evidence remains limited because most studies are small, uncontrolled, retrospective, or based on single clinical cases.

Moreover, the study with the strongest methodological design found no significant reduction in binge-eating episodes with liraglutide compared with placebo, although the medication produced greater weight loss.

Potential Risks: Extreme Dietary Restriction and ED Relapse

Published clinical cases have reported relapse into extreme dietary restriction in people with a history of anorexia nervosa while taking GLP-1 medications. In my clinical practice, I have also met some patients who have developed atypical anorexia nervosa during GLP-1 treatment. The gastrointestinal side effects (e.g., nausea and vomiting) can further complicate the clinical picture, particularly in people who are vulnerable to purging behaviors.

For this reason, the expert group has recommended screening to detect any current or previous eating disorders in all people before starting treatment with GLP-1 medications. This recommendation has reached a 94.7 percent consensus.

When GLP-1 Medications Should Be Avoided, or Used Cautiously

One of the recommendations that reached the highest consensus—100 percent—was to avoid the prescription of GLP-1 medications in people with current diagnoses of atypical anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa associated with a strict dietary restraint and restriction and/or significant weight suppression. The experts also recommended caution in people with a history of these eating disorders. These indications are not absolute contraindications, but they underline that prescribing decisions should not be based exclusively on body weight.

The situation is more complex in people with BED. Although GLP-1 medication, as described above, might be useful for some people with BED, in others they might worsen the eating disorder psychopathology, particularly in the presence of the over-evaluation of shape and weight, significant weight suppression, and marked dietary restriction. These features can negatively affect treatment outcomes and should be assessed before and during medication intake.

Therefore, the expert group has recommended that future studies should assess not only the weight loss and the frequency of binge-eating episodes, but also the dietary restriction, the over-evaluation of shape and weight, and other psychological features of eating disorders.

Reducing “Food Noise” Is Not the Same as Curing an Eating Disorder

The term food noise describes the persistent presence of food and eating thoughts that people often experience as unwanted. GLP-1 medications seem to reduce these thoughts, offering relief to some people.

However, less worrying about food and eating does not necessarily indicate an improvement in eating disorder psychopathology. A person can experience reduced food noise and still adopt extreme, rigid dietary rules, maintaining an intense fear of weight gain or an over-evaluation of shape and weight.

Monitoring During GLP-1 Treatment

The expert group recommended continuous monitoring to detect any appearance or worsening of eating disorder symptoms in people treated with GLP-1 medications. The assessment should include the psychopathology of eating disorders, the weight trend, the food intake, the hunger and satiety levels, the physical condition stability, and the quality of life,

Monitoring intensity should be proportional to individual risk. Frequent monitoring should be planned for people with an eating disorder history, positive screening of eating disorders, rapid weight loss, or a marked suppression of appetite.

One of the most difficult clinical challenges is to distinguish the expected effects of the GLP-1 medication from the developing symptoms of eating disorders. Reduced appetite, smaller meals, and weight loss are expected treatment effects. On the contrary, the onset of rigid and extreme dietary rules, the intense fear of weight gain, or a progressive increase in the over-evaluation of shape and weight can indicate the development or the worsening of the eating disorder psychopathology.

Finally, the expert group recommended associating an evidence-based psychological treatment in people with eating disorders who use GLP-1 medications. This recommendation received an 81.6 percent consensus.

An important issue to be investigated is to evaluate the possibility that GLP-1 medications improve outcomes when they are associated with psychological treatments for BED. However, the available evidence does not support the routine use of these medications in BED treatment.

What Research Should Be Prioritized Next?

The consensus paper has identified several important gaps in the available knowledge.

First, it is necessary to conduct long-term studies to establish whether GLP-1 medications increase, reduce, or do not change the risk of developing an eating disorder.

Second, researchers need reliable methods to distinguish medication-induced appetite changes from pathological dietary restriction.

Third, clinical studies on BED should be designed to evaluate not only binge-eating frequency and weight loss, but also eating disorder psychopathology, dietary restriction severity, food noise, quality of life, nutritional security, and outcomes of suspending pharmacological treatment.

Finally, with the increasing popularity of GLP-1 medications, collaboration between specialists in the treatment of obesity and eating disorders will become increasingly important.

item.title: Why Cats Are More Beautiful Than Us
item.description:
Beauty

Why Cats Are More Beautiful Than Us

And why sexy is not the same as beautiful.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Why do we find almost every cat beautiful, but relatively few humans?
  • Beauty and sexual attractiveness are not the same thing.
  • Like cats, a person may be beautiful without knowing it.
Sita and Sarita (1893–94) by Cecilia Beaux (detail). All animals contain a part of God, but only the cat knows it.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Cecilia Beaux/Public domain

We find every cat, or almost, to be beautiful. But when it comes to other human beings, beauty is more the exception than the rule. We might walk past hundreds of faces without seeing one that makes us look again.

Yet people try a lot harder than cats, expending considerable time, money, and ingenuity on beautifying themselves. We exercise, diet, dress, moisturize, dye, paint, inject, and sometimes even submit to the surgeon’s scalpel. Cats, meanwhile, do little more than lick themselves.

Are we just an uglier species, like bats or warthogs, or might there be more to it than that?

Of Mice and Men

It may be that our aesthetics are a product of our mind. Bats may not be ugly to other bats, and cats probably don’t think of us as ugly—but do seem to think of us as smelly.

Indeed, bats and cats may be entirely without aesthetic judgment and respond merely to mating signals.

But even if we are the only truly aesthetic animal—as argued by the philosopher Immanuel Kant—that does not explain why we find the average cat to be a lot more beautiful than the average member of our own species.

One possibility is that we are more sensitized to human faces. To the untrained eye, all sheep look alike, whereas their shepherd may be able to recognize each one. A large area of our cerebral cortex is devoted to visual processing, with specialized mechanisms for recognizing and reading other human faces.

But should that not mean that we find human faces more, rather than less, beautiful?

Beauty and the Beast

Perhaps the more important difference lies not in what we see, but in what we look for. When we admire a cat, we admire its proportions, coloring, movements, and general appearance. But when we look at another human being, our judgment is complicated by sexual desire, or the absence of it. We are asking not merely whether a face or body is beautiful on its own terms, but whether we find it sexually attractive.

Of course, we can sometimes find a middle-aged body or wizened face beautiful, but this often requires the kind of perceptual shift that we undergo in a museum, when contemplating a work of art.

In a museum, as Kant would tell us, we suspend our ordinary practical judgments and attend to an object for its own sake. We can admire the appearance of Socrates in a David painting, without asking whether his snub nose and pot belly would feed our appetites. Yet we seldom extend the same generosity to people we encounter in everyday life. In a sense, the museum turns us back from animal to human.

Beauty and sexiness are not the same thing. We can find someone beautiful without being attracted to them, and vice versa—which is fortunate for ugly people.

On Youth and Old Age

And young people too. Smooth skin, lustrous hair, and a certain fullness of the face and body are among the qualities we associate with sexual attractiveness. Not every young person is attractive, of course, but youth confers advantages that are difficult to appreciate until they have disappeared.

Indeed, one of the ironies of aging is that we look back at photographs of our younger selves and wonder how we could ever have been dissatisfied—or have made so little of our looks for the few summers that they lasted.

Yet beauty, as opposed to buxomness, need not diminish with age. It is possible to become even more beautiful. An older face may acquire a beauty that depends less on its proportions than on its character and expression. To be beautiful, an older face may also need to be interesting.

Human beauty is not so rare as we suppose. We are simply too distracted by desire, comparison, and convention to appreciate it.

Perhaps we should learn to look at people as we do at paintings, or cats.

Cats are not just beautiful, but irresistibly cute. Part of why we find them so beautiful is simply that we love them.

Cats have no conception of beauty, and certainly no ambition to be beautiful—though they purr when we call them so. They neither admire their reflection nor regret their younger selves. They, like us, simply go on being beautiful, whether we notice or not.

You may also enjoy my companion piece, Why Computers Could Never Experience Beauty.

item.title: A Gift in Ugly Wrapping Paper
item.description:
Self-Help

A Gift in Ugly Wrapping Paper

Discovering wisdom in life’s liminal spaces

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • In a liminal space, former roles, identities, structures, or relationships may no longer fit.
  • The gap between who you were and who you are becoming can feel ambiguous and disorienting.
  • Liminal spaces invite us to create and step into a more aligned way of being in the world.
  • Liminal space transformation tools include: surrendering, non-attachment, and allowing.
Source: Leeloothefirst / Pexels

The Liminal Space Experience

The space between an ending and a new beginning can feel like “a gift wrapped in ugly paper, tied with ribbons of thorns.” It begins with the persistent awareness that something familiar is ending. Roles, identities, relationships, and ways of moving through the world begin to shift, leaving you between the life you have known and the one that has yet to take shape.

What previously provided you with structure and comfort no longer fits or aligns with your deepest values and core needs. You find yourself suspended between who you have been and who you are becoming. The person you are being called to become has yet to be revealed.

Welcome to the liminal or in-between space. Residing in this space can feel excruciatingly ambiguous, painful, and more than a tad disorienting.

In the past, I often responded to the uncertainty of the liminal space by trying to leave it too soon. I would quickly choose a new direction, make a decision, create a plan, and move forward.

Anything felt preferable to remaining with the discomfort. Movement, even movement without clarity, felt energizing and productive and preferable to feeling disempowered and stuck.

With the wisdom of age and experience, I discovered my urgency to escape the discomfort of the liminal space prevented me from uncovering and fully benefiting from its gifts. My avoidance approach was at best merely a temporary respite.

I learned that the discomfort I was attempting to escape was actually inviting me to shed what I had outgrown. The liminal space was calling for me to create and step into a more aligned way of being in the world.

Surrendering, Non-Attachment, and Allowing in the Liminal Space

As I practiced embracing my time in the liminal space, I experienced that purposefully engaging with surrendering and non-attachment served to unwrap the potential gifts offered in this space.

Surrendering does not mean resignation, giving up, postponing critical and timely decisions, or staying in an unhealthy or dangerous situation. Surrendering connotes releasing resistance to what is happening internally while temporarily inhabiting the liminal space.

Surrendering doesn’t require relinquishing responsibility, intention, or agency. It offers an invitation to engage with what is present, rather than risking depletion through fighting with what is out of your realm of control.

Non-attachment does not mean indifference to what lies beyond the liminal space. It means releasing the need for the next chapter to unfold in a particular way or on a preferred timetable. Releasing attachment to a specific outcome makes it possible to increase your openness to previously unanticipated possibilities.

From Surrender to Allowing

Together, surrender and non-attachment invite us to trust our capacity to meet and learn from the emotions that arise in the liminal space. Sitting with these emotions instead of avoiding or rushing past them cultivates a deeper capacity for allowing.

Allowing creates room to:

  • Question old roles, identities, assumptions, values, and expectations.
  • Make time and space to grieve what no longer aligns with who we are becoming.
  • Honor what served us in the past and release what no longer does.
  • Discover and experiment with new ways of being in the world.

Practices for Unwrapping the Gifts of the Liminal Space

What might become possible if you approached your current or next liminal space with curiosity? The following practices can help you remain present, loosen your attachment to certainty, and participate intentionally in what is endeavoring to emerge.

Pause and Discern

  • Recognize the urge to flee. Ask whether you are avoiding discomfort or moving toward something meaningful.
  • Honor the roles, relationships, structures, and ways of being that supported you in the past.
  • Release attachment to a particular timeline or outcome.

Explore What Is Emerging

  • Experiment with small, intentional steps to discover what resonates with your strengths, emerging goals, values, passions, and longings.
  • Schedule time for self-care, reflection, meandering, discovery, and intentional action.
  • Engage with an essential liminal space question: Who am I being called to become?

Liminal Space Wisdom

The inherent gifts of the liminal space rarely arrive fully formed inside the ugly wrapping paper and ribbons of thorns. The gifts are revealed via our willingness to participate in the unwrapping process. Our deepest gift is learning to pause with intention and practice surrender, non-attachment, and allowing. In doing so, we generate the opportunity for the liminal space to transform us, ugly wrapping paper, thorns, and all.

item.title: Why "Night Owls" Are Just as Productive as "Morning Larks"
item.description:
Sleep

Why "Night Owls" Are Just as Productive as "Morning Larks"

It's the duration and quality of sleep that matter.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Sleep duration and quality matter more than whether you wake early or stay up late.
  • Standard work schedules may explain early birds’ mood advantage.
  • Consistent sleep schedules, outdoor exercise, and less bedtime screen use can support better sleep.
Source: Vika Glitter / Pexels

Many prominent people claim an early start to their day is the key to their success. CEOs, world leaders, and influential figures often tout routines involving early mornings. Hustle culture echoes this sentiment, making bold claims about the life-changing benefits of waking up at 4 a.m., even if that means surviving on just four hours of sleep and several cups of coffee. This perspective, however, tends to be shortsighted. Here’s why.

Good Sleep Is About Duration and Quality, Not Bedtimes And Waketimes

Sleep plays a vital role in our cognitive, biological, and psychological functioning. While it’s true that the requirement for sleep decreases as we age, the CDC recommends getting a minimum of seven hours of sleep every 24 hours, even for adults.

So, why is this number important? A 2020 study conducted on 8,698 adults and published in Sleep Medicine observed that when participants deviated from the recommended seven to eight hours, their quality of life dropped. While this drop was found both in participants who slept more and those who slept less, it was especially significant for the latter group. The study also found that deviating from the recommended sleep duration (by either sleeping more or less) led to depressive symptoms.

Beyond the hours we sleep, the quality of our sleep plays a crucial role in our mental health. A 2021 meta-analysis (of 65 trials involving over 8,600 participants) published in Sleep Medicine Reviews looked into whether improving sleep quality could boost mental health. It found that when sleep improved, so did depression, anxiety and rumination. There were also improvements in stress levels and even positive effects on symptoms of psychosis. To top it off, the more sleep quality improved, the better the participants’ mental health became, meaning that a causal link between sleep quality and mental health is likely.

All of this is to say that if you want to be at your best, you need to prioritize sleep. But the question remains:

Who Sleeps Better: A Night Owl or an Early Lark?

As long as you feel rested the following day, it doesn’t matter which camp you fall into. Some of us are naturally programmed to fall asleep later, while others may have a predisposition to go to bed early and rise early. Both are perfectly okay.

Early larks may have a slight edge in terms of experiencing more positive emotions compared to night owls, according to a 2012 study published in Emotion. But a lot of this has to do with how our society follows a “standard daytime.”

To put it in perspective, think about the average person who has to show up to work at nine in the morning. If this person is a night owl, there’s a chance they haven’t got their seven hours of sleep, which can cascade into low mood as the day progresses. In contrast, an early lark is likely to be well-rested and ready to start the day by, say, six in the morning.

Understanding this is just the first step. The next crucial aspect is how we can apply this knowledge to improve our sleep quality. Here are some tips on how we can adapt our habits to achieve better sleep, regardless of whether we’re night owls or early larks.

  • Engage in some form of outdoor exercise every day, preferably in the sun. This helps regulate your body’s natural sleep-wake cycle, known as the circadian rhythm, and can improve your sleep quality by boosting the production of melatonin, a sleep-inducing hormone, in the evening.
  • Avoid looking at screens at least an hour prior to bedtime. The blue light emitted by screens can interfere with the production of melatonin, making it harder for your brain to recognize it’s time to wind down and sleep, which can disrupt your natural sleep cycle.
  • Pick a bedtime that allows you to sleep for seven hours and stick to it every night. Consistently going to bed and waking up at the same time each day helps stabilize your internal clock, improving both the quality and efficiency of your sleep. Irregular sleep patterns can lead to poor sleep quality and drowsiness.

Instead of getting sidetracked by the night owl versus early lark debate, the question you should really be asking is, “Am I getting enough high-quality sleep?” If the answer is no, making small adjustments to your routine can go a long way. Remember, the whole point of sleeping at night is to be ready for the challenges and tasks that lie ahead. A good night’s sleep is a refresh button for your mind, and it really does make all the difference.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: Grandparents and Divorce: How to Help Without Hurting
item.description:
Divorce

Grandparents and Divorce: How to Help Without Hurting

Grandparents can be a safe harbor for children in a divorce.

Posted October 26, 2026

Sharing music or learning to play an instrument is a rewarding way to spend time with your grandchildren.
Source: Mikhail Nilov/pexels

"I had no say when my son divorced his wife," Bella told me. "She was like a daughter to me! My son wanted me to love her when they married, but now he tells me not to even talk to her! And my grandchildren — I’m worried I’ll lose my time with them too, and what about the holidays?" Bella is grieving, but her husband, Andy, is furious. He says “She was terrible to our son, I don’t blame him for leaving her, and the kids should know whose fault this is.”

When your adult child divorces, you and the other grandparents will also feel the deep loss, especially when there are grandchildren.

You grieve the loss of the marriage, your adult child’s suffering, and the loss of the extended family to whom you’d opened your hearts. You think of the memories of family gatherings that you thought would go on forever. You may have grown close to the other in-laws, but most of all, you suffer for the grandchildren. Will they be okay? Will you still see them? How will your relationships change? What can you say or not say to them, and how can you best support them through this family crisis and change?

Most of my writing has focused on the parents, but I have learned through my clients’ and my own experience how important of a role grandparents play in how children weather a divorce.

Grandparents Matter a Lot During a Divorce

Parents going through divorce are suffering a life crisis. Overwhelmed by anger, grief, or worry, they have to deal with complicated, often new, all-consuming logistics, legal matters, and conflict. Most have reduced emotional resources for their children, despite their love and best intentions. Grandparents can offer a safe place to land for the grandchildren, with consistent traditions and a calm environment. Grandparents offer a protective buffer to their grandchildren, but only if they can stay out of the conflict.

Grandparent Pitfalls: Where Things Can Go Wrong

“Blood is thicker than water,” says Andy. “We have to be loyal to our son, and our grandkids should know the truth about who their mom really is.” Of course, it is human nature to feel protective of your adult children, especially if you feel they were wronged in the marriage or in the divorce. Unfortunately, criticizing one of your grandchildren’s parents puts kids in an intolerable, and unhealthy loyalty bind. Kids know that they have both parents in them, and the loyalty test asks them to reject a part of themselves. Healthy children learn to love and accept both parents during a divorce, without having to decide who was right or wrong, or who was the victim or to blame. When a grandparent gives the children the message that they need to choose between their parents, the children become trapped in the middle. Research is clear that one of the most damaging aspects of divorce for kids is feeling trapped in this loyalty bind. Grandparents need to be mindful not to add to this.

Children are at risk of adopting unhealthy roles during divorce, which I have written about previously. Among these roles are being messengers, spies, or investigators. Asking your grandkids what goes on at the other parent’s home, asking them to pass a message, or to report on events there, all are stressful roles for your grandkids, and your relationship with them will feel less safe as a result. Grandparents risk unconsciously questioning their grandkids — as Andy did when he said, “I’m just curious if she’s got a new man in her life!”

Another risk faced by grandparents is when they feel pulled into managing their adult child’s divorce, their finances, or their legal matters. Adult children need to feel confident and capable as they navigate this huge life change. Without fostering dependency, grandparents can offer emotional support and advice, but advice only when it is requested! Offering practical support such as a meal, babysitting, or transportation help is often greatly appreciated.

Bella’s concern about losing time and emotional closeness with grandchildren is supported by research. Contact with grandchildren often drops when shared custody is established, unless the grandparents can maintain a positive connection with both their child and their ex-spouse. This can be challenging when you, like Andy, are pulled to align yourself with one of the parents. Because grandparents have very limited legal rights in the US, a good relationship with both parents is a far more reliable protection than a court order.

What Is a Grandparent to Do?

Now that you know what not to do, here is how you can support your grandchildren.

Hold down the fort, and stay calm in the storm. Keep your home, routines, and traditions as consistent as possible. Continue your regular Sunday dinners, pizza/movie nights, or playtime at the park to let your grandchildren know that some things are not changing.

Speak kindly about both of your grandchildren’s parents, or say nothing at all. If you feel the need to vent, turn to friends or a therapist. It will harm your relationship with your grandchildren if you speak negatively of either of their parents. Andy struggled with this idea and continued to talk about it in therapy for several sessions.

Don’t probe their emotions but give them space to express themselves if they want to. Listen without advising or correcting them. Express empathy: “That sounds really hard,” or something encouraging like, “It will get easier with time.”

Be sure to let the parents take the lead on what they’d like you to say or not say to the kids. Even if you disagree with their rules or their parenting plan, demonstrate respect and support.

Keep the door open to the other parent. Bella struggled with the loss of her daughter-in-law, but let her know that she hoped to be able to stay in the children’s lives. “Maybe eventually we can reconnect more deeply,” she sighed. I encouraged her, and encourage all grandparents, to acknowledge and take care of their own grief, as the ripple effects of divorces cross through all the generations..

In the End

While grandparents can neither prevent nor fix a divorce, they can give their grandchildren something essential: a safe, warm, stable relationship while everything else in their life is in flux.

Months later, Andy was still angry, but he had noticed his granddaughter went quiet whenever he criticized her mom. "I guess I was making her choose, or to feel bad about loving her mom," he said. "I realized this might be a reason she won’t want to come over." Instead, he decided to teach her to play the ukulele, which he’d wanted to do for a long time.

Bella reached out to her former daughter-in-law and told her she hoped they could stay connected for the children's sake. She was relieved. The last time I saw them, Bella and Andy were planning activities for “Grandparent Camp,” a long weekend with their grandchildren, and their former daughter-in-law dropped the kids off herself.
